bond_lifetime_seconds.conditions: E-selectin (CD62E) / ESL-1; surface plasmon resonance at 37 C. SPECIES: MOUSE -- both partners. Kd 62000 nM, koff 4.6 s-1. Cellular off-rate from tether lifetimes under flow: 0.7 s-1 for human leukocyte tethers at 25 C, ~4x slower than the 2.7 s-1 measured here at 25 C. MONOMERIC affinity, deliberately: both papers exclude oligomers by gel filtration, high flow and short injections, because an earlier radiolabel study of P-selectin read ~70 nM and its authors ascribe the difference to a trace of dimers binding multivalently. On a cell the bond is multivalent and stronger, so this is a floor on avidity rather than an estimate of it. koff over the measured range: 1.1 / 1.9 / 2.7 / 4.6 s-1 at 5 / 15 / 25 / 37 C. Affinity is flat with temperature (56-62 uM throughout), so binding is entropically driven -- unusual for a protein-carbohydrate interaction. ESL-1 sits on the LATERAL surfaces of microvilli, not the tips where PSGL-1 and L-selectin are, which fits a role in strengthening rolling rather than first capture.
bond_lifetime_seconds.rationale: 1/koff = 1/4.6 s-1, so it inherits everything the off-rate does: species mouse, 37 C, and a monomeric bond.
bond_lifetime_seconds.source: Wild MK, Huang MC, Schulze-Horsel U, van der Merwe PA, Vestweber D. J Biol Chem 2001;276(34):31602-31612, Tables II-IV

bond_lifetime_seconds.conditions: ICAM-1 (CD54) / LFA-1; surface plasmon resonance at 25 C. SPECIES: HUMAN -- both partners. Kd 500 nM, koff 0.1 s-1. Cellular off-rate from tether lifetimes under flow: not reported; this is the firm-adhesion bond, not a rolling tether, and it has no tether lifetime. MONOMERIC affinity, deliberately: both papers exclude oligomers by gel filtration, high flow and short injections, because an earlier radiolabel study of P-selectin read ~70 nM and its authors ascribe the difference to a trace of dimers binding multivalently. On a cell the bond is multivalent and stronger, so this is a floor on avidity rather than an estimate of it. STATE: Mg2+-INDUCED HIGH-AFFINITY STATE, and that is a choice the authors made: 1 mM Ca2+ cut binding by 20%, so they ran 'in the absence of Ca2+, but in the presence of Mg2+ to induce high affinity state of LFA-1'. LFA-1 on an UNSTIMULATED T cell binds ICAM-1 at about 100 uM -- 200x weaker than this. A resting lymphocyte modelled with 500 nM is wrong by that factor, and this is the only bond in the cascade with two states this far apart. Binding is to D1D2 of ICAM-1 as an IgG chimera; D1D5 has the same potency. Native ICAM-1 is a DIMER, and dimerising soluble ICAM-1 raises affinity for LFA-1 'by two orders of magnitude' -- so the monomeric floor is especially far below the cellular avidity here. Other reported values: 100 nM and 130 nM by receptor-binding assay, 400 nM on phorbol-activated T cells.
bond_lifetime_seconds.rationale: 1/koff = 1/0.1 s-1, so it inherits everything the off-rate does: species human, 25 C, and a monomeric bond.
bond_lifetime_seconds.source: Tominaga Y, Kita Y, Satoh A, Asai S, Kato K, Ishikawa K, Horiuchi T, Takashi T. J Immunol 1998;161(8):4016-4022, Table I

bond_lifetime_seconds.conditions:
L-selectin (CD62L) / GlyCAM-1; surface plasmon resonance at 25 C. SPECIES: RAT CD62L BINDING MOUSE GLYCAM-1 -- A CROSS-SPECIES PAIR, NOT ONE ORGANISM. Kd 108000 nM, koff >=10 s-1. Cellular off-rate from tether lifetimes under flow: ~7 s-1 intrinsic, from L-selectin tethers extrapolated to zero flow, which agrees with this. MONOMERIC affinity, deliberately: both papers exclude oligomers by gel filtration, high flow and short injections, because an earlier radiolabel study of P-selectin read ~70 nM and its authors ascribe the difference to a trace of dimers binding multivalently. On a cell the bond is multivalent and stronger, so this is a floor on avidity rather than an estimate of it. SPECIES, FROM THE PRIMARY SOURCE. PMID:11404363 Table IV lists this interaction as 'Mouse'. It is not: the authors expressed a soluble monomeric RAT CD62L and bound it to GlyCAM-1 purified from MOUSE serum, and flag it themselves -- 'One caveat is that we measured the affinity and kinetics of rat CD62L binding to mouse GlyCAM-1.' They argue it is tolerable because the two CD62L lectin domains are 93% identical. A secondary table simplified it, and this library had taken the simplification.
WHY koff IS A BOUND AND NOT A MEASUREMENT: the observed decay, half-time ~0.07 s, is the time to WASH THE SAMPLE OUT OF THE FLOW CELL, not dissociation -- the control surface falls at the same rate, and the instrument cannot sample faster than 0.1 s. So >=10 s-1 is a floor set by the apparatus. kon >=1e5 is then calculated from one bound and one affinity, so it is a bound too.
HOW FAR THE MONOMERIC FLOOR IS BELOW AVIDITY, measured in this same paper: soluble GlyCAM-1 binding to IMMOBILISED CD62L is detectable at ~30 nM and comes off with koff <=0.001 s-1 -- at least 10,000x slower than the 10 s-1 monovalent rate. That is multivalent binding at serum concentration, and it is how GlyCAM-1 is thought to signal by cross-linking CD62L.
Affinity is flat with temperature (108 +/- 4 uM at 25 C, n=8; 100 +/- 6 at 37 C), so like E-selectin-ESL-1 this bond is entropically driven. If CD62L-CD4 were in fact a dimer the authors note both Kd and koff would be UNDERestimates.
bond_lifetime_seconds.rationale: 1/koff = 1/10 s-1, so it inherits everything the off-rate does: species RAT CD62L binding MOUSE GlyCAM-1 -- a cross-species pair, not one organism, 25 C, and a monomeric bond.
bond_lifetime_seconds.source: Nicholson MW, Barclay AN, Singer MS, Rosen SD, van der Merwe PA. J Biol Chem 1998;273(2):763-770, Tables II and III

koff_per_s.conditions:
L-selectin (CD62L) / GlyCAM-1; surface plasmon resonance at 25 C. SPECIES: RAT CD62L BINDING MOUSE GLYCAM-1 -- A CROSS-SPECIES PAIR, NOT ONE ORGANISM. Kd 108000 nM, koff >=10 s-1. Cellular off-rate from tether lifetimes under flow: ~7 s-1 intrinsic, from L-selectin tethers extrapolated to zero flow, which agrees with this. MONOMERIC affinity, deliberately: both papers exclude oligomers by gel filtration, high flow and short injections, because an earlier radiolabel study of P-selectin read ~70 nM and its authors ascribe the difference to a trace of dimers binding multivalently. On a cell the bond is multivalent and stronger, so this is a floor on avidity rather than an estimate of it. SPECIES, FROM THE PRIMARY SOURCE. PMID:11404363 Table IV lists this interaction as 'Mouse'. It is not: the authors expressed a soluble monomeric RAT CD62L and bound it to GlyCAM-1 purified from MOUSE serum, and flag it themselves -- 'One caveat is that we measured the affinity and kinetics of rat CD62L binding to mouse GlyCAM-1.' They argue it is tolerable because the two CD62L lectin domains are 93% identical. A secondary table simplified it, and this library had taken the simplification.
WHY koff IS A BOUND AND NOT A MEASUREMENT: the observed decay, half-time ~0.07 s, is the time to WASH THE SAMPLE OUT OF THE FLOW CELL, not dissociation -- the control surface falls at the same rate, and the instrument cannot sample faster than 0.1 s. So >=10 s-1 is a floor set by the apparatus. kon >=1e5 is then calculated from one bound and one affinity, so it is a bound too.
HOW FAR THE MONOMERIC FLOOR IS BELOW AVIDITY, measured in this same paper: soluble GlyCAM-1 binding to IMMOBILISED CD62L is detectable at ~30 nM and comes off with koff <=0.001 s-1 -- at least 10,000x slower than the 10 s-1 monovalent rate. That is multivalent binding at serum concentration, and it is how GlyCAM-1 is thought to signal by cross-linking CD62L.
Affinity is flat with temperature (108 +/- 4 uM at 25 C, n=8; 100 +/- 6 at 37 C), so like E-selectin-ESL-1 this bond is entropically driven. If CD62L-CD4 were in fact a dimer the authors note both Kd and koff would be UNDERestimates.
koff_per_s.rationale: Published as a LOWER BOUND, not a point estimate. The decay the instrument saw was the washing time -- how long it takes to clear the sample from the flow cell, half-time ~0.07 s -- and the control surface falls at the same rate, so no dissociation was observed at all. The floor is set by the apparatus, which cannot sample faster than 0.1 s. Stored as a plain number because the library has no way to hold an inequality, which is exactly why the bound is spelled out here.
koff_per_s.source: Nicholson MW, Barclay AN, Singer MS, Rosen SD, van der Merwe PA. J Biol Chem 1998;273(2):763-770, Tables II and III

bond_lifetime_seconds.conditions: ICAM-1 (CD54) / LFA-1; surface plasmon resonance at 25 C. SPECIES: HUMAN -- both partners. Kd 500 nM, koff 0.1 s-1. Cellular off-rate from tether lifetimes under flow: not reported; this is the firm-adhesion bond, not a rolling tether, and it has no tether lifetime. MONOMERIC affinity, deliberately: both papers exclude oligomers by gel filtration, high flow and short injections, because an earlier radiolabel study of P-selectin read ~70 nM and its authors ascribe the difference to a trace of dimers binding multivalently. On a cell the bond is multivalent and stronger, so this is a floor on avidity rather than an estimate of it. STATE: Mg2+-INDUCED HIGH-AFFINITY STATE, and that is a choice the authors made: 1 mM Ca2+ cut binding by 20%, so they ran 'in the absence of Ca2+, but in the presence of Mg2+ to induce high affinity state of LFA-1'. LFA-1 on an UNSTIMULATED T cell binds ICAM-1 at about 100 uM -- 200x weaker than this. A resting lymphocyte modelled with 500 nM is wrong by that factor, and this is the only bond in the cascade with two states this far apart. Binding is to D1D2 of ICAM-1 as an IgG chimera; D1D5 has the same potency. Native ICAM-1 is a DIMER, and dimerising soluble ICAM-1 raises affinity for LFA-1 'by two orders of magnitude' -- so the monomeric floor is especially far below the cellular avidity here. Other reported values: 100 nM and 130 nM by receptor-binding assay, 400 nM on phorbol-activated T cells.
bond_lifetime_seconds.rationale: 1/koff = 1/0.1 s-1, so it inherits everything the off-rate does: species human, 25 C, and a monomeric bond.
bond_lifetime_seconds.source: Tominaga Y, Kita Y, Satoh A, Asai S, Kato K, Ishikawa K, Horiuchi T, Takashi T. J Immunol 1998;161(8):4016-4022, Table I

granule_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
granule_volume_fraction.rationale: One table, one method, one paper, which is what makes the 77-fold spread across these cells a comparison rather than four unrelated numbers. Table 2 as printed, which is an OVERESTIMATE: the paper's Appendix puts the bias from finite section thickness at up to 44% for this cell, so the true fraction is between 0.0014 and 0.0020. Not corrected here because the Appendix states a maximum rather than a point estimate.

microvillus_density_per_um2.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes, 85-90% pure, fixed in suspension and imaged by SEM at 10,000-20,000x; density counted in a 2x2 um box per cell
microvillus_density_per_um2.rationale: 4.1 +/- 1.2 villi/um^2 over 28 cells. Read off the table, and the table is why this changed. It had been 3.0, cited to PMID 27647916 and attributed to that paper's Fig. S2 legend -- but the full text of PMID 27647916, read on 2026-10-21, contains no density at all: no '3 +/- 0.5', no figure per um^2, nothing. The number may be in its supplementary material, which nobody here has seen. Meanwhile the paper this library already cited for microvillus LENGTH states a density for human lymphocytes directly, with n. The old note also called 3.0 'the midpoint of the 2-4 range' from this paper. The 2-4 range is the ABSTRACT's summary across mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line; the human row of Table 2 is 4.1, at the top of it. Taking a midpoint of a cross-species range in place of the human measurement is how a number ends up a quarter low.
microvillus_density_per_um2.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

microvillus_diameter_um.conditions: Resting primary human T cells; SEM. Effector T cells measured 'comparable' in the same paper
microvillus_diameter_um.rationale: Midpoint of a measured 70-100 nm range; the measurement is the range. The 150 nm figure in circulation traces to a review and could not be confirmed in any primary source.

microvillus_length_um.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes; SEM morphometry, individual microvilli traced within a 2x2 um box
microvillus_length_um.rationale: 0.38 +/- 0.22 um over 1,200 microvilli. A MEDIAN of a strongly right-skewed distribution, not a mean. Lengths run 'from 0.1 um to several micrometers' (PMID 27647916, verbatim), so a constant-length coat has the wrong shape and not merely the wrong number. It had been 0.35, which is the midpoint of the 0.3-0.4 range the abstract quotes ACROSS SOURCES -- mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line. The human row of Table 2 is 0.38. Confirmed from an unrelated direction by PMID 6775712, read 2026-10-20: TEM morphometry puts 'the height of the membrane foldings at 305 mosmole' at 'about 0.35 um', and checks it by arithmetic -- a 6.72 um smooth-sphere diameter plus twice the folding height gives 7.42 um, which is what light microscopy measures at the outer edge. Two methods 24 years apart, one measuring villus length and the other folding height, agree to two figures.
microvillus_length_um.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

nuclear_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
nuclear_volume_fraction.rationale: The record reads 'nucleus 44.4%: granules 0.2%: mitochondria 3.8%: cytoplasm 51.6%'. Petrzilka (PMID 308396) agrees independently at 0.458, from 47.5 um^3 of nucleus in a 103.8 um^3 cell. A RADIUS is the cube root of this; using the fraction as a radius gives a nucleus at 8.8% of the cell. The same Appendix that discounts the granule fractions clears this one: the section-thickness error is 'negligible, because the section thickness is small in comparison to nuclear dimensions'. Checked against the paper's own Table 1, where an eosinophil nucleus of 37 um^3 in a 206 um^3 cell is 18.0% against Table 2's 17.9%.

microvillus_length_um.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

nuclear_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
nuclear_volume_fraction.rationale: The record reads 'nucleus 44.4%: granules 0.2%: mitochondria 3.8%: cytoplasm 51.6%'. Petrzilka (PMID 308396) agrees independently at 0.458, from 47.5 um^3 of nucleus in a 103.8 um^3 cell. A RADIUS is the cube root of this; using the fraction as a radius gives a nucleus at 8.8% of the cell. The same Appendix that discounts the granule fractions clears this one: the section-thickness error is 'negligible, because the section thickness is small in comparison to nuclear dimensions'. Checked against the paper's own Table 1, where an eosinophil nucleus of 37 um^3 in a 206 um^3 cell is 18.0% against Table 2's 17.9%.

granule_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
granule_volume_fraction.rationale: One table, one method, one paper, which is what makes the 77-fold spread across these cells a comparison rather than four unrelated numbers. Table 2 as printed, which is an OVERESTIMATE: the paper's Appendix puts the bias from finite section thickness at up to 44% for this cell, so the true fraction is between 0.0014 and 0.0020. Not corrected here because the Appendix states a maximum rather than a point estimate.

It had been 3.0, cited to PMID 27647916 and attributed to that paper's Fig. S2 legend -- but the full text of PMID 27647916, read on 2026-10-21, contains no density at all: no '3 +/- 0.5', no figure per um^2, nothing. The number may be in its supplementary material, which nobody here has seen. Meanwhile the paper this library already cited for microvillus LENGTH states a density for human lymphocytes directly, with n. The 2-4 range is the ABSTRACT's summary across mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line; the human row of Table 2 is 4.1, at the top of it. Taking a midpoint of a cross-species range in place of the human measurement is how a number ends up a quarter low.

migration_speed_um_per_min.conditions: Normal human dermal fibroblasts and 20 other cell types, tracked by Hoechst-stained nuclei at 37 C and fitted as a persistent random walk (Fuerth model). THE SPEED IS THE MODE, NOT THE CELL: mesenchymal 0.234+/-0.09; amoeboid A1 1.7+/-0.4; amoeboid A2 (stable bleb) 5.3+/-1.5 um/min, all measured on the same cell types. The switch is triggered by 3 um confinement plus the absence of focal adhesions, which is why this matters for a tumour: the authors argue the confinement imposed by surrounding tissue 'might be enough to trigger a migratory switch toward a faster and more invasive mode of migration'. The 0.234 figure is the UNCONFINED 2D adherent regime and must not be read into a confined one.
migration_speed_um_per_min.rationale:
Figure 4C, the mesenchymal control. The number was already correct; its conditions came from a BioNumbers record rather than the paper, and the sentence stored as its rationale is about EPITHELIAL cells -- an adjacent paragraph that BioNumbers picked up.
What was missing is the finding: the same cells reach 1.7 um/min (A1) and 5.3 um/min (A2) once confined to 3 um without focal adhesions. Twenty-three fold, with no genetic change. A confined tissue simulation that reads 0.234 is using the one regime the paper excludes.
migration_speed_um_per_min.source: Liu YJ, Le Berre M, Lautenschlaeger F, Maiuri P, Callan-Jones A, Heuze M, Takaki T, Voituriez R, Piel M. Cell 2015;160(4):659-672, Figure 4C

sourced.migration_model: Persistent random walk (Fuerth): MSD(t) = 2 S P (t - P(1 - exp(-t/P))), D = S^2 P / 2. Speed alone does not give a diffusion coefficient; persistence is the other half, and the two trade off with adhesion. PMID:25679760

amoeboid_a1.environment: 3 um confinement on a non-adhesive surface, LOW contractility: a round body with a small leading edge, driven by a retrograde actin flow localised to that protrusion

amoeboid_a2.environment: 3 um confinement on a non-adhesive surface, HIGH contractility: an elongated body with a uropod, driven by a GLOBAL cortical retrograde flow. Every leukocyte tested adopted this mode, and so did every transformed cell line

mesenchymal.environment: 2D adherent culture, unconfined: focal adhesions, stress fibres, spindle shape

granule_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
granule_volume_fraction.rationale: One table, one method, one paper, which is what makes the 77-fold spread across these cells a comparison rather than four unrelated numbers. Table 2 as printed, which is an OVERESTIMATE: the paper's Appendix puts the bias from finite section thickness at up to 44% for this cell, so the true fraction is between 0.0014 and 0.0020. Not corrected here because the Appendix states a maximum rather than a point estimate.

microvillus_density_per_um2.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes, 85-90% pure, fixed in suspension and imaged by SEM at 10,000-20,000x; density counted in a 2x2 um box per cell
microvillus_density_per_um2.rationale: 4.1 +/- 1.2 villi/um^2 over 28 cells. Read off the table, and the table is why this changed. It had been 3.0, cited to PMID 27647916 and attributed to that paper's Fig. S2 legend -- but the full text of PMID 27647916, read on 2026-10-21, contains no density at all: no '3 +/- 0.5', no figure per um^2, nothing. The number may be in its supplementary material, which nobody here has seen. Meanwhile the paper this library already cited for microvillus LENGTH states a density for human lymphocytes directly, with n. The old note also called 3.0 'the midpoint of the 2-4 range' from this paper. The 2-4 range is the ABSTRACT's summary across mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line; the human row of Table 2 is 4.1, at the top of it. Taking a midpoint of a cross-species range in place of the human measurement is how a number ends up a quarter low.
microvillus_density_per_um2.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

microvillus_diameter_um.conditions: Resting primary human T cells; SEM. Effector T cells measured 'comparable' in the same paper
microvillus_diameter_um.rationale: Midpoint of a measured 70-100 nm range; the measurement is the range. The 150 nm figure in circulation traces to a review and could not be confirmed in any primary source.

microvillus_length_um.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes; SEM morphometry, individual microvilli traced within a 2x2 um box
microvillus_length_um.rationale: 0.38 +/- 0.22 um over 1,200 microvilli. A MEDIAN of a strongly right-skewed distribution, not a mean. Lengths run 'from 0.1 um to several micrometers' (PMID 27647916, verbatim), so a constant-length coat has the wrong shape and not merely the wrong number. It had been 0.35, which is the midpoint of the 0.3-0.4 range the abstract quotes ACROSS SOURCES -- mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line. The human row of Table 2 is 0.38. Confirmed from an unrelated direction by PMID 6775712, read 2026-10-20: TEM morphometry puts 'the height of the membrane foldings at 305 mosmole' at 'about 0.35 um', and checks it by arithmetic -- a 6.72 um smooth-sphere diameter plus twice the folding height gives 7.42 um, which is what light microscopy measures at the outer edge. Two methods 24 years apart, one measuring villus length and the other folding height, agree to two figures.
microvillus_length_um.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

nuclear_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
nuclear_volume_fraction.rationale: The record reads 'nucleus 44.4%: granules 0.2%: mitochondria 3.8%: cytoplasm 51.6%'. Petrzilka (PMID 308396) agrees independently at 0.458, from 47.5 um^3 of nucleus in a 103.8 um^3 cell. A RADIUS is the cube root of this; using the fraction as a radius gives a nucleus at 8.8% of the cell. The same Appendix that discounts the granule fractions clears this one: the section-thickness error is 'negligible, because the section thickness is small in comparison to nuclear dimensions'. Checked against the paper's own Table 1, where an eosinophil nucleus of 37 um^3 in a 206 um^3 cell is 18.0% against Table 2's 17.9%.

nonlethal_contact_minutes.conditions: Human: resting NK cells from healthy-donor buffy coats, on HEK293T targets, time-lapse microscopy over 8 h. Conjugation is scored as "the NK cell assumes a rounded morphology with membrane flattening at the site of intercellular contact", distinct from a following "attachment" phase in which it "remains attached to the target cell but visibly seeks to migrate away". "On average, activated NK cells remained conjugated to target cells twice as long (65 vs. 29 min, p < 0.005) ... as resting NK cells."
nonlethal_contact_minutes.rationale: The 29 min is the mean conjugation of RESTING NK cells, which in this assay "showed a significantly lower ability to kill HEK293T cells than activated cells" -- so their conjugations are predominantly the non-lethal ones, which is the quantity wanted. It is the committed conjugate, not any touch: a study scoring contact as bare co-localization of the two cells reports most NK-target interactions as transient, under 4 min (PMID:27323411), and those brushes are encounters a simulation filters out at recognition rather than contacts it times. Longer than the 19 min lethal contact, as expected -- a synapse that fails to kill is the more stable one (perforin-null CTL synapses persist for hours, PMID:37500886). In 3D collagen the comparable activated-NK figure is 47.9 min against 65 min in 2D (PMID:31337806), so a value in tissue is likely somewhat lower than this 2D one.
nonlethal_contact_minutes.source: Olofsson PE et al., Front Immunol 2014 (PMC3945532)

migration_speed_um_per_min.source: BioNumbers BNID:112247 (Butler KL et al., Burn injury reduces neutrophil directional migration speed in microfluidic devices. PLoS One. 2010 Jul)

radius_um.conditions: Unactivated human peripheral blood neutrophils, isolated by plasma-Percoll and counterflow elutriation, measured in suspension at 22 C. Flow cytometry (axial pulse extinction, calibrated against 5/10/15 um latex beads): mean of three donors 8.33 um, individual cells 7.04-10.25 um, 11,000-70,000 cells per donor. The same donors by Coulter counter read 8.40 um; the flow figure is used because the authors lead with it and name a bias in the other ('overestimation of cell volume due to plasma trapping in the surface folds'). RUFFLE-INCLUSIVE: this is the functional diameter including membrane folds, which is larger than the ruffle-excluded morphometry in PMID:6775712 that this library uses for granule volume fractions.
radius_um.rationale:
Table 1, flow cytometry column, mean of three donors: 8.333 um diameter -> 4.167 um radius. The paper's own text rounds this to '8.33', which is how the transcription here was checked.
This replaces a stored 4.2 um that was already graded MEASURED against this same PMID before the paper was read. 4.2 is the COULTER mean (8.40 um diameter), not the flow mean the authors lead with, and nothing recorded which of the two it was.
radius_um.source: Downey GP, Doherty DE, Schwab B 3rd, Elson EL, Henson PM, Worthen GS. J Appl Physiol 1990;69(5):1767-1778, Table 1

sourced.diameter_convention: ruffle-inclusive (functional), per PMID:2272970; the granule fractions in this library are ruffle-excluded, PMID:6775712

granule_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
granule_volume_fraction.rationale: One table, one method, one paper, which is what makes the 77-fold spread across these cells a comparison rather than four unrelated numbers. microvillus_density_per_um2.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes, 85-90% pure, fixed in suspension and imaged by SEM at 10,000-20,000x; density counted in a 2x2 um box per cell
microvillus_density_per_um2.rationale: 4.1 +/- 1.2 villi/um^2 over 28 cells. Read off the table, and the table is why this changed. It had been 3.0, cited to PMID 27647916 and attributed to that paper's Fig. S2 legend -- but the full text of PMID 27647916, read on 2026-10-21, contains no density at all: no '3 +/- 0.5', no figure per um^2, nothing. The number may be in its supplementary material, which nobody here has seen. Meanwhile the paper this library already cited for microvillus LENGTH states a density for human lymphocytes directly, with n. The old note also called 3.0 'the midpoint of the 2-4 range' from this paper. The 2-4 range is the ABSTRACT's summary across mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line; the human row of Table 2 is 4.1, at the top of it. Taking a midpoint of a cross-species range in place of the human measurement is how a number ends up a quarter low.
microvillus_density_per_um2.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

microvillus_diameter_um.conditions: Resting primary human T cells; SEM. Effector T cells measured 'comparable' in the same paper
microvillus_diameter_um.rationale: Midpoint of a measured 70-100 nm range; the measurement is the range. The 150 nm figure in circulation traces to a review and could not be confirmed in any primary source.

microvillus_length_um.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocytes; SEM morphometry, individual microvilli traced within a 2x2 um box
microvillus_length_um.rationale: 0.38 +/- 0.22 um over 1,200 microvilli. A MEDIAN of a strongly right-skewed distribution, not a mean. Lengths run 'from 0.1 um to several micrometers' (PMID 27647916, verbatim), so a constant-length coat has the wrong shape and not merely the wrong number. It had been 0.35, which is the midpoint of the 0.3-0.4 range the abstract quotes ACROSS SOURCES -- mouse, human and a B-lymphoma line. The human row of Table 2 is 0.38. Confirmed from an unrelated direction by PMID 6775712, read 2026-10-20: TEM morphometry puts 'the height of the membrane foldings at 305 mosmole' at 'about 0.35 um', and checks it by arithmetic -- a 6.72 um smooth-sphere diameter plus twice the folding height gives 7.42 um, which is what light microscopy measures at the outer edge. Two methods 24 years apart, one measuring villus length and the other folding height, agree to two figures.
microvillus_length_um.source: Majstoravich S et al., Blood 2004;104(5):1396-1403, Table 2

nuclear_volume_fraction.conditions: Human peripheral blood lymphocyte; stereology on electron micrographs
nuclear_volume_fraction.rationale: The record reads 'nucleus 44.4%: granules 0.2%: mitochondria 3.8%: cytoplasm 51.6%'. Petrzilka (PMID 308396) agrees independently at 0.458, from 47.5 um^3 of nucleus in a 103.8 um^3 cell. A RADIUS is the cube root of this; using the fraction as a radius gives a nucleus at 8.8% of the cell. The same Appendix that discounts the granule fractions clears this one: the section-thickness error is 'negligible, because the section thickness is small in comparison to nuclear dimensions'. Checked against the paper's own Table 1, where an eosinophil nucleus of 37 um^3 in a 206 um^3 cell is 18.0% against Table 2's 17.9%.

kcat_per_s.conditions: Cleaved caspase-8 homodimer, active-site titrated, in 20 mM Tris / 100 mM NaCl pH 7.4 at 37 C -- the paper's LOW-SALT buffer. Substrate Ac-IETD-AFC at 100 uM. kcat 0.65 +/- 0.1 s^-1.
kcat_per_s.rationale:
Table 1, the row measured under near-physiological salt. It had been 0.88, graded DERIVED, as 'the median of 4 BRENDA measurements across 1 papers, spanning 0.65 to 1.25'. Reading the table shows those four are not four measurements of one thing:
  0.65  cleaved caspase-8 homodimer, low salt      <- this one
  1.25  the SAME enzyme in 0.7 M sodium citrate
  0.98  caspase-8/FLIP-L HETERODIMER, 0.7 M citrate
  0.78  the same heterodimer with FLIP-L D297A
Three different molecular species, and three of the four in a kosmotrope. Sodium citrate at 0.7 M is not a cellular condition: the paper uses it as a tool to force dimerization -- 'capable of salting out proteins from solution, creating local areas of high protein concentration' -- and says it improved Km and kcat 'probably due to stabilization of the active site'. Taking the median across them averages a homodimer with a heterodimer and physiological salt with a laboratory device.
kcat_per_s.source: Boatright KM et al., Biochem J 2004;382:651-657, Table 1

km_ietd_um.conditions: Cleaved caspase-8 homodimer, active-site titrated, in 20 mM Tris / 100 mM NaCl pH 7.4 at 37 C -- the paper's LOW-SALT buffer. Substrate Ac-IETD-AFC at 100 uM. Km 55.2 +/- 2.0 uM.
km_ietd_um.rationale:
55.2 +/- 2.0 uM on Ac-IETD-AFC, the same row as the kcat so the pair describes one enzyme under one condition. In 0.7 M sodium citrate the same enzyme reads 20.6 uM, which is the size of the kosmotrope's effect on Km alone.
Stored under the substrate-named alias, not as a bare km_um: Ac-IETD-AFC is a fluorogenic TETRAPEPTIDE. It reports on the active site, and it is not BID or procaspase-3. A Km for a real protein substrate is a different measurement and this one must not stand in for it.
km_ietd_um.source: Boatright KM et al., Biochem J 2004;382:651-657, Table 1

copies_per_cell.calibrated_against: 25,000 PSGL-1 (CD162) copies on a human Neutrophil (PMID:9829984)
copies_per_cell.conditions: 64.8 ppm of total protein molecules in Macrophage, measured in peripheral blood monocytes; cell volume 4989 um^3 from its evidenced radius. 2.2e+06 protein molecules per um^3, fixed by 25,000 PSGL-1 (CD162) copies on a Neutrophil of 303 um^3 (PMID:9829984) at 37.5 ppm. CHECK: this predicts 5.3e+09 proteins in a HeLa cell of 2425 um^3, against a literature range of 2e+09-1e+10.
copies_per_cell.rationale:
A ppm is a RATIO and cannot become a count without knowing how many molecules a cell holds. The scale comes from one absolute measurement rather than a sourced protein density -- the obvious BioNumbers record for that turned out to be 'number of proteins PRODUCED per cell', a flux and not a census.
CALIBRATED, not MEASURED, and the weakest link is named: PaxDb has no Neutrophil dataset for PSGL-1 (CD162), so the anchor's ppm is the Monocyte value as the nearest myeloid proxy. Every count here inherits that assumption, which has been checked: CZ CELLxGENE Census 2025-01-30 (blood, primary): mean SELPLG counts 1.001/cell in 43,430 neutrophils vs 0.468-1.177 across 1.64M monocytes, ratio 0.85. Transcript, not protein, and neutrophil scRNA-seq drops out badly (46% positive), so this supports the substitution without establishing it.
Stored for Macrophage, where this receptor is most abundant of the cells whose size is evidence. The per-cell-type counts are in sourced['copies_per_cell'] -- averaging a count across cells of different volumes would mean nothing.
TOTAL cellular copies, not surface. On the membrane alone this many would cover 1.3% of it, which is small enough that a large surface fraction is at least possible. surface_density_per_cell is left untouched; the surface fraction is its own measurement and this library has it for nothing.
copies_per_cell.source: PaxDb abundance scaled by one absolute count; see cognisom/library/seed_copy_numbers.py

copies_per_cell.calibrated_against: 25,000 PSGL-1 (CD162) copies on a human Neutrophil (PMID:9829984)
copies_per_cell.conditions: 2.67 ppm of total protein molecules in Memory B cell, measured in peripheral blood B cells; cell volume 116 um^3 from its evidenced radius. 2.2e+06 protein molecules per um^3, fixed by 25,000 PSGL-1 (CD162) copies on a Neutrophil of 303 um^3 (PMID:9829984) at 37.5 ppm. CHECK: this predicts 5.3e+09 proteins in a HeLa cell of 2425 um^3, against a literature range of 2e+09-1e+10.
copies_per_cell.rationale:
A ppm is a RATIO and cannot become a count without knowing how many molecules a cell holds. The scale comes from one absolute measurement rather than a sourced protein density -- the obvious BioNumbers record for that turned out to be 'number of proteins PRODUCED per cell', a flux and not a census.
CALIBRATED, not MEASURED, and the weakest link is named: PaxDb has no Neutrophil dataset for PSGL-1 (CD162), so the anchor's ppm is the Monocyte value as the nearest myeloid proxy. Every count here inherits that assumption, which has been checked: CZ CELLxGENE Census 2025-01-30 (blood, primary): mean SELPLG counts 1.001/cell in 43,430 neutrophils vs 0.468-1.177 across 1.64M monocytes, ratio 0.85. Transcript, not protein, and neutrophil scRNA-seq drops out badly (46% positive), so this supports the substitution without establishing it.
Stored for Memory B cell, where this receptor is most abundant of the cells whose size is evidence. The per-cell-type counts are in sourced['copies_per_cell'] -- averaging a count across cells of different volumes would mean nothing.
TOTAL cellular copies, not surface. On the membrane alone this many would cover 0.0% of it, which is small enough that a large surface fraction is at least possible. surface_density_per_cell is left untouched; the surface fraction is its own measurement and this library has it for nothing.
copies_per_cell.source: PaxDb abundance scaled by one absolute count; see cognisom/library/seed_copy_numbers.py

replication_cycle_hours.conditions: Six serosusceptible adults inoculated intranasally with 10^4.2 TCID50 of cloned wild-type A/Hong Kong/123/77 (H1N1); daily nasal wash titres fitted with a target-cell-limited model carrying an eclipse phase. Geometric mean of six patient-specific fits; 95% CI 4.6-7.9 h. UPPER respiratory tract -- the authors note natural infection also involves the lower tract, where the kinetics may differ.
replication_cycle_hours.rationale:
1/k in Table 3: the time from a cell being infected to that cell releasing its first virion, the eclipse phase. Confirmed on reading the paper, which states it in words -- 'it takes about 6 h between infection of target cells and virion release'.
Two neighbouring quantities in the same table are NOT this one, and a reader reaching for 'the replication cycle' could take either by mistake: 1/delta = 4.6 h is how long a cell goes on PRODUCING virus once it starts, and <t> = 11.4 h is the whole lifetime of an infected cell, eclipse plus production. The paper itself rounds that last one to 'about 12 h'.
The free-virion half-life from the same fit is 3.2 h (CI 1.9-5.3) and R0 is 22 (CI 10-46); neither is stored and both could be.
replication_cycle_hours.source: Baccam P et al., J Virol 2006;80(15):7590-7599, Table 3

retracted.name: IgA1 (secretory)
retracted.why: An IGH* accession translates to ONE heavy-chain constant region. Stored as the antibody's molecular weight it was wrong by 3x to 19x -- IgM (pentameric) read 51.9 kDa against a real ~970. The chain mass is kept as constant_region_mass_kda; the assembled mass is not recorded, because this library has no source for it.
